B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P01 · STOP / CHOOSE

ICE IS NOT A SHORTCUT

Assess before the first step — no gear means a land route

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
A frozen surface is not a travel route until its condition is independently evaluated.

FIELD ACTION

1
Stop at the shorelineDo not step onto unknown lake, river, marsh, or pond ice.
2
Identify current and transitionsLook for culverts, inlets, outlets, narrows, open water, and flooded shorelines.
3
Ask what you can actually verifyWithout measurement gear, known conditions, and escape equipment, select a land route.
4
CommunicateTell your group the route and update a reliable contact if you can.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Stop at the shoreline — Do not step onto unknown lake, river, marsh, or pond ice.
  2. Identify current and transitions — Look for culverts, inlets, outlets, narrows, open water, and flooded shorelines.
  3. Ask what you can actually verify — Without measurement gear, known conditions, and escape equipment, select a land route.
  4. Communicate — Tell your group the route and update a reliable contact if you can.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Everybody remains on stable shore terrain.
  • A land detour or shelter plan is identified.
  • No one interprets another person’s tracks as proof.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Tracks across a lakePast travel does not prove current ice strength.
A cold night after a thawRefreezing at the surface does not verify underlying strength.
No way aroundShelter, signal and reassess rather than guess.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P02 · IDENTIFY / REJECT

RECOGNIZE ICE TYPES

Appearance is a warning tool, never permission to cross

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
New, clear ice is generally stronger than white, refrozen, thawed or deteriorated ice, but strength is not visible with certainty.

FIELD ACTION

1
Identify the surface classNote clear, white, slush-covered, layered, or deteriorated ice.
2
Check the seasonFreeze-thaw, sun, snow cover, and spring weakening change strength.
3
Treat unknown layers as unknownA smooth-looking surface can conceal weak layers.
4
Reject uncertaintyDo not replace actual thickness measurement with color or sound.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Identify the surface class — Note clear, white, slush-covered, layered, or deteriorated ice.
  2. Check the season — Freeze-thaw, sun, snow cover, and spring weakening change strength.
  3. Treat unknown layers as unknown — A smooth-looking surface can conceal weak layers.
  4. Reject uncertainty — Do not replace actual thickness measurement with color or sound.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Photo identification is treated as preliminary only.
  • Suspect slush, dark water and thaw conditions trigger a route change.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

White surface looks solidSnow ice can be weaker than new clear ice.
No cracks or soundsAbsence of noise does not establish safety.
Ice looks black or clearVisual clarity cannot replace measurement.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P03 · MAP / AVOID

FIND THE WEAK ZONES

Current and transition areas can undermine ice locally

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
Water beneath the surface is moving. Ice can thin rapidly where that water flows, warms or meets a structure.

FIELD ACTION

1
Locate inflows and outflowsMark creeks, springs, outlets, culverts and drainage channels.
2
Locate bottlenecksAvoid narrows, bridges and channels with currents.
3
Inspect edges from shoreShore ice, reeds and overflow can conceal weak transitions.
4
Plan without crossingRoute on stable ground; do not approach open leads or pressure ridges.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Locate inflows and outflows — Mark creeks, springs, outlets, culverts and drainage channels.
  2. Locate bottlenecks — Avoid narrows, bridges and channels with currents.
  3. Inspect edges from shore — Shore ice, reeds and overflow can conceal weak transitions.
  4. Plan without crossing — Route on stable ground; do not approach open leads or pressure ridges.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Potential current zones are excluded from the route.
  • Map and visible terrain are reconciled before movement.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

One thickness measurementIce can differ sharply nearby.
Bridge or culvert shortcutFlowing water can thin ice unexpectedly.
A pressure ridge looks solidBreaks and refrozen cracks are unstable transition areas.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P04 · NO EQUIPMENT

NO-GEAR WINTER DETOUR

Worst-case response when you cannot verify the ice

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
A stick, footprints, an animal track or a frozen shoreline is not a valid substitute for measured ice conditions.

FIELD ACTION

1
Choose safe groundLook for a route around the waterbody, not across it.
2
Check the detourAvoid steep banks, unstable snow, open channels and hidden marsh water.
3
Limit unnecessary travelIf the detour increases exposure beyond your capacity, find shelter and make yourself visible.
4
Signal and documentUse a phone or high-contrast ground marker when available.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Choose safe ground — Look for a route around the waterbody, not across it.
  2. Check the detour — Avoid steep banks, unstable snow, open channels and hidden marsh water.
  3. Limit unnecessary travel — If the detour increases exposure beyond your capacity, find shelter and make yourself visible.
  4. Signal and document — Use a phone or high-contrast ground marker when available.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • All water crossings remain excluded.
  • The group can describe its next safe decision.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Try breaking thin ice with a branchNo improvised probing method establishes safe load capacity.
Follow a snowmobile trailPrevious users may have had knowledge or equipment you lack.
Keep moving while lostEscalate to shelter and rescue instead of compounding exposure.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P05 · MEASURE / RECHECK

IF EQUIPPED: CHECK FIRST

Minnesota DNR minimums are screening guidance, not a guarantee

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
Minnesota DNR says to consider on-foot travel only after measuring at least 4 in (10 cm) of new, clear ice — and even then ice is never guaranteed safe.

FIELD ACTION

1
Pre-plan with another personShare route, time and emergency plan. Avoid solitary travel.
2
Wear proper flotation and carry ice picksKeep rescue tools immediately accessible.
3
Drill or chisel a hole; measureUse a tape to measure actual clear ice thickness, not surface snow.
4
Recheck along the routeConditions change; reject current, white ice, thaw or unmeasurable locations.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Pre-plan with another person — Share route, time and emergency plan. Avoid solitary travel.
  2. Wear proper flotation and carry ice picks — Keep rescue tools immediately accessible.
  3. Drill or chisel a hole; measure — Use a tape to measure actual clear ice thickness, not surface snow.
  4. Recheck along the route — Conditions change; reject current, white ice, thaw or unmeasurable locations.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Measurement is repeated; no single spot stands for the lake.
  • A local expert and route-specific hazards have been checked.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

A chisel did not break throughResistance is not a substitute for tape measurement.
4 inches measured onceNot proof that the entire route meets the guidance.
Forgot flotation or picksReturn for proper equipment; do not improvise safety.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P06 · SELF-RESCUE

IF YOU BREAK THROUGH

Turn back, kick horizontal, pull out, roll away

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
Cold shock can disrupt breathing immediately. Keeping your airway above water and escaping promptly are the first priorities.

FIELD ACTION

1
Control breathing; keep clothing onDo not waste time stripping winter layers in the water.
2
Face the direction you camePlace arms on unbroken ice; use picks if available.
3
Kick to become horizontalDrive forward while pulling your torso onto the ice.
4
Lie flat and roll awayReturn toward your approach path. Seek warm shelter immediately.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Control breathing; keep clothing on — Do not waste time stripping winter layers in the water.
  2. Face the direction you came — Place arms on unbroken ice; use picks if available.
  3. Kick to become horizontal — Drive forward while pulling your torso onto the ice.
  4. Lie flat and roll away — Return toward your approach path. Seek warm shelter immediately.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Clear of the weak edge before standing.
  • 911/medical help initiated as soon as possible.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Cannot lift onto the iceKeep airway up; call for help and continue controlled attempts if possible.
Ice breaks againFollow the approach direction; stay spread flat.
Exhaustion or reduced movementUrgent rescue is needed; cold-water incapacitation can develop rapidly.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P07 · BYSTANDER

IF SOMEONE ELSE FALLS IN

Call 911 — help from stable ground — do not rush the edge

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
A second person entering weak ice can double the emergency. Use shore-based rescue and keep everyone else away.

FIELD ACTION

1
Call 911 immediatelyGive the exact waterbody and access location, number of people, and visible condition.
2
Talk to the personEncourage them to face their approach path and keep their airway above water.
3
Reach or throw from safetyOffer a long object, rope or flotation device only without entering weak ice.
4
Move everyone away from the edgeLeave ice entry to trained rescuers; keep communicating.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Call 911 immediately — Give the exact waterbody and access location, number of people, and visible condition.
  2. Talk to the person — Encourage them to face their approach path and keep their airway above water.
  3. Reach or throw from safety — Offer a long object, rope or flotation device only without entering weak ice.
  4. Move everyone away from the edge — Leave ice entry to trained rescuers; keep communicating.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Rescuer remains on secure ground.
  • Dispatch has an accurate location and live updates.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Running to the holeYou risk creating a second victim.
Pulling from unstable footingStop if you may be pulled in; do not approach.
Pet falls throughDo not enter the ice; notify responders.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P08 · COLD-WATER RECOVERY

AFTER THE WATER

Protect the core, limit heat loss, obtain medical help

STAGED SCENE • NOT A RELIABLE ICE-CONDITION IDENTIFICATION PHOTO
Escaping the water is not the end of the emergency. Drowning complications and hypothermia can emerge during recovery.

FIELD ACTION

1
Get to shelter and call for helpGet out of wind, wet snow and continued cold exposure.
2
Replace saturated clothing as feasibleWrap in dry insulation; cover head/neck and isolate from ground.
3
Rewarm the body carefullyUse insulated warmth around the torso if available. Handle the person gently.
4
Monitor responsiveness and breathingCall emergency services for confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness or unresponsiveness.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Get to shelter and call for help — Get out of wind, wet snow and continued cold exposure.
  2. Replace saturated clothing as feasible — Wrap in dry insulation; cover head/neck and isolate from ground.
  3. Rewarm the body carefully — Use insulated warmth around the torso if available. Handle the person gently.
  4. Monitor responsiveness and breathing — Call emergency services for confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness or unresponsiveness.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • The person is protected from wind and the ground.
  • Medical escalation is arranged for any significant immersion, injury, symptoms or breathing concern.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Give drinks to confused personDo not provide food or fluids if swallowing is unsafe.
Direct high heat / rubbing limbsAvoid burns, tissue damage and harmful rewarming of extremities.
Assume shivering means wellResponsiveness and mental status matter more than shivering alone.
STOP CONDITION: If ice strength cannot be verified, stay off. If someone has fallen through, summon emergency responders immediately.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P09 · SPRING / SHORELINE

THAWED ICE: NO SHORTCUT

Spring warmth, water and wind can destroy load capacity long before the lake looks open.

STAGED ILLUSTRATION • NOT A FIELD-VERIFIED ICE OR RESCUE PHOTOGRAPH
Treat thawing, waterlogged or seasonally deteriorating ice as impassable.

FIELD ACTION

1
Stop at stable landDo not walk out to inspect the ice edge. Shorelines may be undercut or detached.
2
Scan from shoreLook for open seams, water on ice, soft edges, movement and wind-driven breakup.
3
Reject the spring crossingOld or partially thawed ice can fail despite considerable apparent thickness.
4
Change the routeDetour on land, shelter if necessary, or call for help rather than test it with your body.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Stop at stable land — Do not walk out to inspect the ice edge. Shorelines may be undercut or detached.
  2. Scan from shore — Look for open seams, water on ice, soft edges, movement and wind-driven breakup.
  3. Reject the spring crossing — Old or partially thawed ice can fail despite considerable apparent thickness.
  4. Change the route — Detour on land, shelter if necessary, or call for help rather than test it with your body.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Everyone remains off the ice and away from weak banks.
  • Route does not depend on a thin shore connection.
  • Wind, rain and daytime thaw are considered.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Surface looks frozenRecent thaw/refreeze is not evidence of underlying strength.
Tracks lead acrossEarlier crossings are not verification.
Open water near bankDo not approach an overhanging or detached edge.
STOP CONDITION: Spring deterioration, open water or thaw/refreeze history: do not enter. Choose land access.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P10 · SNOW / OVERFLOW

SNOW CAN HIDE THE HOLE

A white cover hides cracks, slush, overflow and thickness changes.

STAGED ILLUSTRATION • NOT A FIELD-VERIFIED ICE OR RESCUE PHOTOGRAPH
Do not use dry-looking snow as a proxy for strong ice.

FIELD ACTION

1
Evaluate from landIdentify slush bands, dark/wet patches, overflow and concealed stream outlets.
2
Recognize insulationSnow can slow ice growth. Heavy snow can also load the ice.
3
Separate snow from iceRefrozen surface snow (white ice) is not equivalent to new clear ice.
4
Select a dry-land alternativeIf the layer beneath cannot be inspected and measured, do not travel across.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Evaluate from land — Identify slush bands, dark/wet patches, overflow and concealed stream outlets.
  2. Recognize insulation — Snow can slow ice growth. Heavy snow can also load the ice.
  3. Separate snow from ice — Refrozen surface snow (white ice) is not equivalent to new clear ice.
  4. Select a dry-land alternative — If the layer beneath cannot be inspected and measured, do not travel across.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • No one uses a pole poke as proof of safe travel.
  • Snow-covered drainage routes and culverts are treated as hazards.
  • No numeric ice-strength claim is inferred from appearance.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

It held yesterdayConditions and snow loading can change rapidly.
Snow crust is hardA strong crust does not measure ice underneath.
Puddles are shallowOverflow/slush may hide weak ice and openings.
STOP CONDITION: Hidden ice condition, slush, overflow, current or snow cover without measurement: remain off.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P11 · VARIABILITY

ONE HOLE DOES NOT CLEAR A ROUTE

Thickness and strength can change over short distances, especially around current.

STAGED ILLUSTRATION • NOT A FIELD-VERIFIED ICE OR RESCUE PHOTOGRAPH
A local measurement is a point observation—not a route certification.

FIELD ACTION

1
Start with the ruleMinnesota DNR’s 4-inch (10 cm) guideline is for new clear ice on foot, never a guarantee.
2
Identify variabilityConsider springs, inlets, narrows, currents, vegetation decay and snow load.
3
Use correct tools onlyIce checks require suitable measurement equipment and trained judgement, not guesswork.
4
Abort uncertain travelWithout equipment and a rescue plan, use land instead of trying to prove safe ice.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Start with the rule — Minnesota DNR’s 4-inch (10 cm) guideline is for new clear ice on foot, never a guarantee.
  2. Identify variability — Consider springs, inlets, narrows, currents, vegetation decay and snow load.
  3. Use correct tools only — Ice checks require suitable measurement equipment and trained judgement, not guesswork.
  4. Abort uncertain travel — Without equipment and a rescue plan, use land instead of trying to prove safe ice.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • “New clear ice” limitation remains on all thickness numbers.
  • Old, white, thawed or current-affected ice is not rated by the same simple rule.
  • Retreat or stay ashore is a real option.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

4 inches at one pointNearby ice may be much thinner.
Four inches of white iceDNR clear-ice guidance does not transfer directly.
Someone else is fishingTheir location does not verify your route.
STOP CONDITION: If any segment cannot be evaluated, do not cross.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P12 · FAMILY / PETS

KEEP CHILDREN & PETS ON LAND

Prevent a rescue emergency instead of responding to one.

STAGED ILLUSTRATION • NOT A FIELD-VERIFIED ICE OR RESCUE PHOTOGRAPH
Children and animals must not approach unknown ice to investigate or retrieve objects.

FIELD ACTION

1
Establish a shore boundaryKeep children close and dogs leashed where frozen water is accessible.
2
Explain the hazardA snow-covered pond, stream or ditch may look like ground.
3
Do not chaseIf a pet goes onto the ice, do not follow onto unknown ice.
4
Call for helpCall 911 when a person is at risk or in the water; keep bystanders on land.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Establish a shore boundary — Keep children close and dogs leashed where frozen water is accessible.
  2. Explain the hazard — A snow-covered pond, stream or ditch may look like ground.
  3. Do not chase — If a pet goes onto the ice, do not follow onto unknown ice.
  4. Call for help — Call 911 when a person is at risk or in the water; keep bystanders on land.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Kids and pets stay on firm land away from edges.
  • A responsible adult maintains continuous supervision.
  • There is no ice-edge approach for a dropped toy or runaway dog.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Dog walks acrossAnimal weight cannot establish a human-safe route.
Ice looks like a snow fieldHidden water and moving currents remain possible.
Rescuer runs after petCall trained responders; do not create a second victim.
STOP CONDITION: No one steps onto unknown ice for a pet, toy or shortcut.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P13 · 911 / LOCATION

CALL EARLY. BE EASY TO FIND.

Reliable location and access information can be as important as rescue equipment.

STAGED ILLUSTRATION • NOT A FIELD-VERIFIED ICE OR RESCUE PHOTOGRAPH
If someone breaks through or is trapped, call 911 immediately from a safe location.

FIELD ACTION

1
Call 911Report ice immersion or stranded people and say whether anyone is still in the water.
2
Give a precise locationLake or river name, access/road name, landmarks and GPS coordinates if available.
3
Report what responders needNumber of people, observable condition, openings/currents and where crews can access land.
4
Stay accessibleFollow dispatcher directions, keep your phone warm, and use visible signals from safe ground.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Call 911 — Report ice immersion or stranded people and say whether anyone is still in the water.
  2. Give a precise location — Lake or river name, access/road name, landmarks and GPS coordinates if available.
  3. Report what responders need — Number of people, observable condition, openings/currents and where crews can access land.
  4. Stay accessible — Follow dispatcher directions, keep your phone warm, and use visible signals from safe ground.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • Dispatcher has your location and the best land access.
  • Group stays out of weak-ice rescue zones.
  • Backup signaling is considered if phone service fails.

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

“We are on a lake”Provide a named access point and distinct landmark.
No cellular signalUse a carried PLB/SOS device if available; signal from shore.
Call ends earlyStay available for callbacks where possible.
STOP CONDITION: Do not delay calling while searching for gear or attempting an ice-edge rescue.

B013 · MINNESOTA ICE SAFETY · P14 · PRACTICE ON LAND

REACH / THROW: PRACTICE DRY

Learn the movement on stable ground; ice-water rescue itself requires professional training.

STAGED ILLUSTRATION • NOT A FIELD-VERIFIED ICE OR RESCUE PHOTOGRAPH
A rehearsal is useful only when it does not expose anyone to water or unsafe ice.

FIELD ACTION

1
Choose a safe training areaUse dry, level ground with a cone or stationary target; no frozen pond required.
2
Practice communicationOne participant calls “911” in the scenario; another directs the team from a safe position.
3
Practice a controlled throwToss a rescue bag or appropriate soft line toward the target while maintaining stable footing.
4
Inspect and resetCheck line handling, no tangling around fingers or neck, and repeat with a qualified instructor.

HOW THE DECISION OR ACTION WORKS

  1. Choose a safe training area — Use dry, level ground with a cone or stationary target; no frozen pond required.
  2. Practice communication — One participant calls “911” in the scenario; another directs the team from a safe position.
  3. Practice a controlled throw — Toss a rescue bag or appropriate soft line toward the target while maintaining stable footing.
  4. Inspect and reset — Check line handling, no tangling around fingers or neck, and repeat with a qualified instructor.

CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING

  • All participants and the target remain on dry land.
  • No participant wraps rope around limbs or throat.
  • Every drill rehearses “do not go onto weak ice.”

WRONG SIGNAL → CORRECTION

Tangled ropeRepack the line; inspect before another practice throw.
Thrower steps forwardReset the safe position and rehearse stable balance.
Someone suggests live-water practiceStop; use instructor-led specialized rescue training.
STOP CONDITION: Never turn this dry-land drill into a self-directed ice or open-water rescue exercise.
